explanations.answer: Ahab's silver and gold and his family
explanations.explanation: Ben-hadad, king of Aram, sends word to Ahab, king of Israel: “Your silver and gold are mine, and your best wives and children are mine!” (1 Kings 20:3) Silver, gold, family. That's the whole list. Ben-hadad doesn't ask nicely, either.

explanations.answer: Ahab's horses and chariots and his land
explanations.explanation: Horses and chariots do show up in this story, friend, but they come with the thirty-two kings on Ben-hadad's side (1 Kings 20:1). His message to Ahab, king of Israel, is about something else. He names silver, gold, and the best wives and children. Nobody in that message says a word about land.

explanations.answer: Ahab's fields and flocks and his cities
explanations.explanation: Fields, flocks and cities sound like what a conqueror would want, so I get the guess. But that's not on Ben-hadad's list. His message says, “Your silver and gold are mine, and your best wives and children are mine!” Ahab, king of Israel, hears silver, gold, and family.

explanations.answer: He agrees to all of it
explanations.explanation: Ahab says, “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” That's a yes to everything on the list. I think saying that out loud with an army outside had to be a rough moment. Hold onto it, because Ahab's answer changes when the second message comes.

explanations.answer: He refuses every bit of it
explanations.explanation: Not this time. Ahab's first answer is a yes: “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” The no comes later, and only to the second demand (1 Kings 20:9). So Ahab starts out going along, then draws a line.

explanations.answer: He asks for a few days to think
explanations.explanation: No stalling here. The text just says the king of Israel replied, and what he says is, “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” Ahab doesn't ask for a single day to think. It's a yes, and it covers everything Ben-hadad asked for.

A whole week would be a gift, friend, but that's not what the message says. Ben-hadad says, “But about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to search your palace…” Tomorrow. Most people can't even get a plumber to show up that fast.

Right, no week at all. Ben-hadad says, “But about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to search your palace…” That's one day. His servants will search the palace and the houses of Ahab's servants, and they'll carry away what is precious to Ahab.

Ahab summons “…all the elders of the land…” He tells them Ben-hadad is looking for trouble, because Ahab didn't deny him a single thing in the first demand. Smart move, calling in the whole table before answering.

The prophet does show up in this story, but not here. He approaches Ahab later, in verse 13, with a word from the LORD. For this moment, the text says Ahab “…summoned all the elders of the land…” Elders first, prophet later.

Priests aren't in this scene. The text says Ahab “…summoned all the elders of the land…” (1 Kings 20:7). He tells them that Ben-hadad is looking for trouble. I like how a king with an army outside the walls still stops to ask for advice.

The elders and the people all say, “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” That's a clear answer from everybody at the table. Ahab had already said yes to the first demand, and now the elders and the people tell him to refuse these terms. I think it's a crowd that has had enough.

That's what Ahab already did the first time, and the elders and the people go the other way. They say, “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” So the answer is don't listen, not give in. Nobody in that room is signing the next paper.

explanations.answer: Pay him to leave the city
explanations.explanation: Paying him off isn't on the table. The elders and the people say, “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” That's not a bargain, friend. It's a no, and it's about as plain as a no gets.

Ahab keeps his first yes. He tells the messengers, “All that you demanded of your servant the first time I will do, but this thing I cannot do.” The silver, gold, wives and children stay on the yes side. Only the second demand, the search of the palace, gets the no.

Right, Ahab doesn't take anything back. He says, “All that you demanded of your servant the first time I will do, but this thing I cannot do.” His yes to the first demand stands. The no is only for the second demand.

Ben-hadad swears, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” That's his threat: not enough dust left of Samaria for each of his men to take a handful. That's a lot of threat packed into one sentence. Remember that he's the one doing the swearing.

Ben-hadad isn't planning to move in. His oath says, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” He's talking about dust, not a throne. He means to tear Samaria down.

explanations.answer: It'll be spared if Ahab bows
explanations.explanation: There's no offer to spare anything in this message. Ben-hadad swears, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” Nothing about bowing, nothing about a deal. Just dust.

The text says Ben-hadad got Ahab's message “…while he and the kings were drinking in their tents…” That's thirty-three kings, counting Ben-hadad, in tents with cups. I think it's worth noticing where they are when that message reaches them. Hold that picture, because it comes back later in the story.

Resting sounds peaceful, but that's not the word. The text says Ben-hadad received the message “…while he and the kings were drinking in their tents…” So the kings are in their tents, and they're drinking. Quiet naps don't come into it.

Praying? Not in this tent, friend. Ben-hadad received Ahab's message “…while he and the kings were drinking in their tents…” The kings are in their tents, and that's the word the text gives: drinking.

Ben-hadad hears Ahab's message and tells his servants, “Take your positions.” So they station themselves against the city. No long speech, no second oath. Just orders, and his servants take their places.
It is true, friend. After he gets Ahab's message, Ben-hadad says to his servants, “Take your positions.” They station themselves against the city. He answers with orders instead of a reply.

explanations.answer: Deliver it into Ahab's hand this very day
explanations.explanation: A prophet comes to Ahab with a word from the LORD: “Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.” This very day, friend. The army that looked like the end of Samaria is the one the LORD says He'll hand over. Quite a turn from the dust oath.

explanations.answer: Send it back home to Aram
explanations.explanation: That's a quiet ending, but it's not what the prophet says. He brings this word from the LORD: “Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.” The LORD says He will deliver the army into Ahab's hand. And He says it happens today.

explanations.answer: Let it take the city for a while
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say anything about letting the city fall for a while. The prophet says, “Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.” Into Ahab's hand, and this very day. The word comes straight, with no waiting.

explanations.answer: The young officers of the district governors
explanations.explanation: Ahab asks, “By whom?” and the prophet answers, “This is what the LORD says: ‘By the young officers of the district governors.’…” So the LORD names the young officers who serve under the governors of the districts. Not the whole army, not the top brass. I think Ahab had to take a breath at that answer.

explanations.answer: The elders and the people of the land
explanations.explanation: The elders and the people did give Ahab advice earlier, but they're not the answer here. The prophet says, “This is what the LORD says: ‘By the young officers of the district governors.’…” That's the group the LORD names. The elders had their say, and now the young officers get the call.

explanations.answer: A band of prophets of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Only one prophet shows up in this scene, and he's the one delivering the message. When Ahab asks, “By whom?” he hears, “This is what the LORD says: ‘By the young officers of the district governors.’…” No band of prophets is mentioned. The work goes to those young officers.

Ahab asks, “Who will start the battle?” and the prophet answers, “You will.” So the king himself starts it. He's the one who just said yes to every demand on the first list. Now the one who gave in is the one who starts the fight.

The elders told Ahab not to give in, but they don't start the battle. Ahab asks who will, and the prophet says, “You will,” meaning Ahab himself. The elders gave the advice, and the king gets the job.

Ben-hadad's men are in position around the city, so I get why you'd pick him. But Ahab asks who will start the battle and the prophet answers, “You will,” meaning Ahab. Later we see the Israelites marching out of Samaria first. Ahab is the one who starts it.

The young officers go out first, but they don't go alone. After them Ahab assembles the rest of the Israelite troops, 7,000 in all. And when the officers march out of the city, the army is right behind them. So it's 232 up front with a whole army following.

The 232 are in front, but they have company. Ahab assembles “…the rest of the Israelite troops, 7,000 in all.” The text says the army is behind the young officers as they march out of the city. It's a small crew up front, with a bigger one at their backs.

That's the picture, friend. The text says they marched out at noon “…while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were in their tents getting drunk.” Thirty-three kings, in the tents, at noon. It's the same tents we saw earlier.

It is true, and it's right there in the text. Ahab's troops marched out at noon “…while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were in their tents getting drunk.” Midday, and the kings are in their tents. Meanwhile Israel's troops are already marching out.

Ben-hadad tells his men, “If they have marched out in peace…” he said, “take them alive. Even if they have marched out for war, take them alive.” Peace or war, the order is the same. I think that's a king who is sure of himself. Keep that in mind when we see how things go.

explanations.answer: Strike them down at the gate
explanations.explanation: That would be the usual order, but Ben-hadad says something different. He tells his men, “If they have marched out in peace…” he said, “take them alive. Even if they have marched out for war, take them alive.” Alive, not struck down. The order is the same whether the men come for peace or for war.

explanations.answer: Pull back and let them pass
explanations.explanation: Ben-hadad isn't backing off. He says, “If they have marched out in peace…” he said, “take them alive. Even if they have marched out for war, take them alive.” That's capture, not retreat. His men are told to grab them.

Each of the young officers strikes down his opponent, “So the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit.” The word is fled. The Arameans were the ones with the big army and the oath about dust. Now they're the ones running.

Regrouping isn't what the text says. After each of the young officers strikes down his opponent, “…the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit.” They run, and Israel chases. That's the word the text gives: fled.
Surrender isn't what happens. The text says the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit. That's running, not giving up. And remember, Ben-hadad had ordered his men to take Israel's men alive.
Ben-hadad isn't captured. The text says he “…escaped on horseback with the cavalry.” He gets away on a horse while his men run. His army scatters, and the king takes the fast way out.

Right, nobody takes him captive. As the Arameans flee, Ben-hadad king of Aram “…escaped on horseback with the cavalry.” He's the one who had told his men to take others alive. Now he's the one riding away, and the story isn't done with him yet.
